dataDisclaimer: Fares converted at nominal Jan 2026 exchange rates, not purchasing power parity. Chinese fare data from official metro operator websites. Hong Kong data from MTR Corporation.

funding.label: Funding model & farebox recovery
funding.description: Share of operating costs covered by passenger fares. Comparisons are directional — accounting boundaries (capital vs operating, dedicated taxes counted as 'revenue' or not) vary by system.

nyc.ownership: Public — MTA, a NY State public-benefit corporation
nyc.model: Heavily subsidized public agency. Operating revenues (fares + dedicated taxes) ~$19B in 2024; operating expenses ~$22B. Subway-only farebox recovery was >50% pre-pandemic. New congestion-pricing toll (launched Jan 2025) is a major dedicated revenue stream for capital.
nyc.fareRevenueShare: ~25% of MTA operating revenue is from passenger fares; the rest comes from dedicated taxes (payroll mobility tax, real estate taxes, congestion-pricing tolls) and state/city subsidies.
nyc.source: NY State Comptroller / MTA financial reports

london.ownership: Public — Transport for London (TfL), GLA functional body
london.model: Fares cover 53.1% of operating costs in FY2025 (53.3% in FY2024). The rest comes from a central-government grant, business rates retention, the London Congestion Charge, advertising, and property revenue. TfL must cover operating costs from operating revenues per its funding settlement.
london.fareRevenueShare: ~72-73% of total revenue is operating revenue (fares dominate); remainder is grant funding, congestion charge, business rates.
london.private: Private bus operators run TfL-branded services under contract; tube/rail operated by TfL directly.

paris.ownership: Public — IDFM (Île-de-France Mobilités) is the regional authority; RATP and SNCF operate under contract
paris.model: Fares cover ~37% of IDFM's €11.5B operating budget in 2024. The largest single funding source is the *versement mobilité* — a payroll tax on Île-de-France employers with 11+ workers — followed by fare revenue and state/regional contributions.
paris.fareRevenueShare: Fare revenue: €4.3B in 2024. Versement mobilité (employer tax): €6.4B. State + regional contributions: €1.8B.
paris.private: Operations being progressively opened to competitive tendering (buses already, metro/rail from 2025-2040).

tokyo.ownership: Mixed — Tokyo Metro (TSE-listed since Oct 2024; majority state + Tokyo Metropolitan Govt owned) + Toei (Tokyo Metropolitan Govt) + private railways (JR East, Tokyu, etc.)
tokyo.model: Operationally profitable. Tokyo Metro historically reported 119–161% farebox recovery; Toei subway lines also profitable. Capital costs partly financed through ancillary revenues (real estate, retail in stations) on the Japanese private-railway model.
tokyo.fareRevenueShare: Fares are the dominant revenue source; non-fare income (real estate, retail, advertising) is significant but secondary on the subway side.
tokyo.private: JR East (privatized 1987, TSE-listed) and private railways (Tokyu, Odakyu, Keio, etc.) run most commuter rail. Tokyo Metro IPO completed Oct 2024.
tokyo.source: Farebox recovery ratio comparisons (Tokyo Metro published financials)

seoul.ownership: Public — Seoul Metropolitan Rapid Transit + KORAIL (state-owned)
seoul.model: Heavily subsidized. Seoul Metro reported large operating losses in 2022-2023; the 2024 Climate Card (unlimited monthly pass at ~$48) is expected to widen the operating deficit further but is treated as a public-policy investment.
seoul.fareRevenueShare: Fares are the primary direct revenue source but do not cover operating costs; Seoul Metropolitan Government covers shortfalls.
seoul.private: Some new lines operated under PPP concessions (Shinbundang Line, Line 9 sections).

beijing.ownership: Public — Beijing Subway operator (state-owned) + MTR Beijing JV on certain lines
beijing.model: Heavily subsidized. ~11% of operating expenses go to security staff alone (2022). Fares are kept artificially low as a public-policy tool; municipal government covers the shortfall.
beijing.fareRevenueShare: Estimated ~30-50% of operating costs covered by fares; precise published farebox recovery not available.
beijing.private: Hong Kong's MTR Corp operates Line 4 and Daxing Line via 30-year JV with Beijing Infrastructure Investment.
beijing.source: South China Morning Post on China metro economics

shanghai.model: Heavily subsidized. Distance-based fares with low base price (~¥3) keep affordability high; municipal government covers operating shortfall. Significant capital investment continues.
shanghai.fareRevenueShare: Estimated ~40-60% of operating costs from fares; precise published farebox recovery not available.
shanghai.source: Shanghai Shentong Metro Group annual reports (in Chinese)

hongkong.ownership: Mixed — MTR Corporation, HKEX-listed but ~75% owned by Hong Kong SAR Government
hongkong.model: Profitable on fares alone (historical farebox recovery 187%). The famous 'Rail plus Property' model: HK government grants MTR land development rights at pre-railway values; MTR develops housing, retail, and offices around stations and uses the proceeds to fund rail capital. Net profit doubled to HK$15.77B in 2024, with property development contributing HK$10.26B of that.
hongkong.fareRevenueShare: Fares are ~37% of total MTR revenue; property rental, management, and development contribute the rest. For every £1 of ticket revenue, MTR collected ~£0.60 in property/commercial income (2019).
hongkong.private: Publicly traded on HKEX; minority private shareholders. Operates lines in Beijing, Shenzhen, London (Elizabeth line until 2025), Stockholm, Sydney via subsidiaries.
hongkong.source: MTR Corp 2024 annual results; Centre for Cities analysis
